prompt.brief: Design a distributed message-queue service for reliable asynchronous communication, supporting acknowledgements, redelivery, dead-letter handling, ordering, priorities, and consumer backpressure.
successSignals: Define queue, exchange/topic, routing, acknowledgement, visibility timeout, retention, and delivery semantics explicitly.
Replicate durable messages and metadata, partition hot queues, and apply producer and consumer backpressure.
Make redelivery and duplicate consumption safe with consumer idempotency, dead-letter queues, and poison-message isolation.
Explain ordering versus throughput, rebalancing, node loss, quotas, replay, and tenant authorization.

functional: Create queues and bindings, publish messages, consume with leases or acknowledgements, retry failures, and dead-letter poison messages.
Expose queue depth, oldest-message age, consumer lag, delivery attempts, throughput, and retention state.
Support tenant quotas, authentication, replay, message TTL, priority policy, ordering keys, and administrative purge.
nonFunctional: Target p95 publish acknowledgement below 20 ms for replicated durable messages and bounded consumer delivery latency.
Handle millions of messages per second through partitioned queues, batching, replication, and per-tenant quotas.
Never lose an acknowledged durable message; treat delivery as at-least-once and require consumer idempotency.
Apply backpressure and preserve queued messages when consumers or replicas are degraded.
scaleAssumptions: Support 5 million messages per second, 100,000 queues, and bursts from thousands of producers.
Partition by queue and ordering key, split hot queues, and isolate large tenants and slow consumers.
Retain durable messages according to queue policy while keeping delivery leases and consumer presence bounded.

deepDives.title: Consistency and idempotency
points: Keep the Distributed message-queue service commit authoritative; let derived projections converge with visible version and freshness.
Use idempotency keys, conditional Distributed message-queue service writes, event IDs, and versions so retries and replay are safe.
Return Distributed message-queue service version and observedAt so clients can reason about freshness.

deepDives.title: Partitioning and hot keys
points: Partition Distributed message-queue service by its primary read and write keys, then isolate hot tenants, users, items, or regions.
Bound Distributed message-queue service work with backpressure and queue isolation so one hot key cannot dominate the cluster.
Keep a replay or reconciliation path for Distributed message-queue service projection drift and partial failures.

deepDives.title: Failure and recovery
points: Serve the last acceptable Distributed message-queue service projection or an explicit degraded response when workers fail.
Retain durable Distributed message-queue service records for replay and make each downstream effect independently retryable.
Measure Distributed message-queue service latency, backlog, freshness, error rate, and correctness drift.

tradeoffs.title: Strong consistency versus throughput
tradeoffs.recommendation: Strongly protect the business commit and use versioned eventual projections for high-volume reads.
tradeoffs.caution: Making every derived read synchronous increases coordination and tail latency.

tradeoffs.title: Push versus pull processing
tradeoffs.recommendation: Push bounded events to workers and pull durable snapshots on reads or recovery.
tradeoffs.caution: Unbounded fanout or full scans make bursts and hot keys expensive.

tradeoffs.title: Managed service versus custom control
tradeoffs.recommendation: Start with managed primitives where their limits match the access pattern, then isolate replaceable interfaces.
tradeoffs.caution: Provider defaults do not remove the need for quotas, replay, observability, and data lifecycle design.

commonMistakes: Putting all work on the synchronous request path.
Choosing a data store before writing the access patterns and consistency contract.
Ignoring retries, duplicate events, late data, deletion, privacy, or authorization.
Leaving hot partitions, backpressure, stale reads, and recovery unspecified.
Allowing unbounded requests or exports to compete with normal traffic.

followUps.question: What happens when the primary worker is unavailable?
followUps.answer: Acknowledge only after the durable boundary, serve the last acceptable projection, queue retryable work, and replay or reconcile after recovery.

followUps.question: How would you support a tenfold traffic spike?
followUps.answer: Pre-scale partitions, apply admission control and backpressure, isolate hot keys, cache immutable snapshots, and make freshness degradation visible.

followUps.question: How do you verify correctness?
followUps.answer: Use idempotency metrics, version gaps, sampled source-to-projection comparisons, replay tests, and a shadow rebuild before repair.
